description: Enforce strong password policies (length, complexity, history, expiration).
Enable account lockout policies after multiple failed login attempts.
Remove or disable unused software, services, and legacy components.
Restrict local administrator rights and use standard accounts for daily work.
Enable and configure Windows Defender Firewall with restrictive inbound rules.
Block inbound traffic by default and only allow required ports and applications.
Enable automatic Windows Updates or manage updates centrally (e.g. WSUS/SCCM).
Apply critical security patches in a timely manner on all workstations and servers.
Enable advanced audit policies (logon events, privilege use, object access).
Forward security logs to a central logging or SIEM solution for correlation.
Implement regular backups of critical data and system configurations.
Store backups in a separate location and protect them from direct access and ransomware.
Enforce strong password policies using PAM (length, complexity, history).
Disable direct root login over SSH (`PermitRootLogin no`).
Remove unnecessary packages, services, and daemons from the system.
Set secure default file permissions and configure restrictive `umask` values.
Enable a host-based firewall (e.g. `ufw`, `firewalld`, or `iptables`).
Deny incoming traffic by default and only allow required services.
Regularly apply security patches using the distribution's package manager.
Subscribe to distribution security advisories and track critical vulnerabilities.
Enable and retain system logs using `rsyslog`, `journald`, or similar.
Monitor authentication logs (e.g. `/var/log/auth.log`) for suspicious activity.
Implement automated backups for critical data and configuration files.
Store backups on separate systems or storage with restricted access.
Use unique, strong credentials for all administrative interfaces.
Restrict access to admin panels by IP range or VPN when possible.
Keep the web server (e.g. Nginx, Apache) and OS fully patched.
Remove default files, demo applications, and unused modules.
Enforce HTTPS for all web traffic and redirect HTTP to HTTPS.
Disable obsolete protocols and weak ciphers in the TLS configuration.
Set a strict Content-Security-Policy (CSP) to control allowed content sources.
Validate and sanitize all user inputs on the server side.
Use prepared statements/parameterized queries for all database access.
Enable detailed access and error logging on the web server.
Forward logs to a centralized log management or SIEM solution.
Implement regular backups of web content, configuration, and databases.
Store backups securely, offsite or in a separate environment from production.
Enforce phishing-resistant MFA for every console user, and always for root / global administrator accounts.
Lock down root and break-glass accounts: no access keys, hardware MFA, sealed credentials and alerting on any use.
Never expose management ports (SSH, RDP, database ports) directly to the internet; use a bastion or zero-trust access.
Block public access to object storage at organization level; allow exceptions only through documented approval.
Enable control-plane audit logging in every account, subscription and region, stored immutably.
Centralize security logs in a dedicated, access-restricted security account or workspace.
Encrypt sensitive data at rest and enforce TLS 1.2+ for all data in transit.
Keep backups of critical workloads in a separate account with immutability (object lock / vault lock).
Apply organization-level guardrails (policies / SCPs) that prevent disabling logging or using unapproved regions.
Implement an administrative tiering model (Tier 0 / 1 / 2) and prevent Tier 0 credentials from touching lower tiers.
Reduce Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins and Schema Admins to a minimal, named membership with no daily use.
Administer Tier 0 only from dedicated privileged access workstations (PAW).
Deploy Windows LAPS so that every machine has a unique, rotated local administrator password.
Rotate the krbtgt account password (twice) periodically and immediately after a suspected compromise.
Use group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA) wherever the application supports them.
Give accounts with an SPN long random passwords (25+ characters) to defeat Kerberoasting.
Disable and then remove inactive user and computer accounts on a defined schedule.
Patch domain controllers promptly and keep them dedicated (no additional roles or software).
Forward domain controller security logs to the SIEM with adequate audit policy coverage.
Alert on any change to privileged groups, GPOs linked to domain controllers and AdminSDHolder.
